sections.excerpt: Before You Try to Go Deep Reparenting needs enough adult capacity to pause, compare options, remain in the present, and act. When somebody is flooded or identified almost completely with a frightened child-state, those capacities can be hard to reach. The immediate task may be outside support and regulation. Deeper dialogue can wait. Spirit and Mind Health

I love using one foot to massage the other foot like a Ying/Yang symbol, but you ca
sections.heading: Regulation May Come Before Dialogue

sections.excerpt: Somatic Modalities Strategic Sequencing Roadmap u-dont-exist.com · 10 juin Trauma healing is rarely a matter of simply revisiting painful memories. For many people, especially those with complex or developmental trauma, lasting recovery follows a sequence: first establishing safety and nervous system regulation, then releasing accumulated stress and survival
sections.heading: Somatic Modalities Strategic Sequencing Roadmap

sections.excerpt: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult Some people can close their eyes, imagine a loving parent, and immediately feel the archetype. Others summon the voice of the person who shamed, controlled, ignored, or frightened them. Some feel nothing. The instruction “be your own loving parent” already assumes the capacity they are missing.
sections.heading: Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult

sections.excerpt: A Witness Is Enough to Begin The first adult position may be only a witness: “A frightened younger state is here, and something can notice it.” You don’t need warmth, wisdom, or a perfect answer yet. The fact that one part can observe another creates a little space around total identification. Using your own name can help. Instead of “I am terrified,” try, “
sections.heading: A Witness Is Enough to Begin

sections.excerpt: Borrow One Function at a Time A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine. Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it: a therapist, grandmother, teacher, friend, older sibling, spiritual figure, fictional character, future self, or another presence whose care does not require you to disappear. Borrowed Nurturer: “How would this pers
sections.heading: Borrow One Function at a Time

sections.excerpt: Borrow Love and Perspective You Already Have Sometimes the missing capacity is not love itself. You can love other people or animals easily, but the feeling becomes inaccessible or unsafe when the recipient is you. Think of a pet, a baby, a friend, your own child, a partner, or anyone you naturally love. Feel the actual love first, without immediately trying
sections.heading: Borrow Love and Perspective You Already Have

sections.excerpt: Become the Adult Apprentice The borrowed adult should stand beside you rather than replace you. The movement is: receive care → observe care → participate in care → initiate care → internalize care . After a therapist, peer, friend, or imagined figure helps, ask: What did they do that felt warm, protective, or wise? Which five percent of that can I do myself
sections.heading: Become the Adult Apprentice

sections.excerpt: The Three Adult Functions I call the deeper therapy pl/ork : play + work. Calling it only “work” forgets the inner child, who also wants to play. Most people are stuck identifying as the inner child, which can leave them wandering helplessly through adult life from the place that feels small, frightened, abandoned, impulsive, or helpless. Reparenting begins
sections.heading: The Three Adult Functions

sections.excerpt: Make the Protector Visible Set one boundary. Say no to something costly. Handle an avoided task or financial mess. Leave a relationship that keeps eroding safety. Keep one small promise. Clean your room. These acts accumulate into trust because internal soothing without external competence can sound like the same unreliability that wounded the child. When th
sections.heading: Make the Protector Visible

sections.excerpt: When Love Is There but Doesn’t Feel Safe Sometimes love is available and still feels unsafe because the younger state distrusts the person offering it. It looks at the grown-up life it can see—old promises, continuing self-attack, repeated failures of protection—and treats that as evidence. The child thinks it already has a track record to judge, and it does
sections.heading: When Love Is There but Doesn’t Feel Safe

sections.excerpt: Make a Simple Vow When promises still carry some credibility, a quiet vow can help. You can make it with or without a visualization of the two of you playing on a swing: “I know you’re in there. I know I’ve ignored you, and I know you don’t trust me. That’s okay. You don’t have to do anything. My job, starting today, is to build a life that is safe for you.
sections.heading: Make a Simple Vow

sections.excerpt: Give the Vow a Physical Reminder You can give the promise a physical place in the room: a childhood toy, familiar stuffed animal, visible self-love note, or another object that feels steady and kind. Choose what it means while you’re sober and regulated. Let it remind you of the Nurturer or Protector you’re practicing becoming. It doesn’t speak for the child
sections.heading: Give the Vow a Physical Reminder

sections.excerpt: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake This is where many people get stuck. You activate the Nurturer, try to speak to the inner child, and get silence. Or numbness. Or a voice saying, “This is so silly.” Suddenly the phone needs checking, dinner needs planning, and a minor household task becomes emotionally urgent. My friend Scott said: “Half the time when I try t
sections.heading: When the Adult Voice Feels Fake

sections.excerpt: The Parent You Inherited Before you deliberately build the Nurturer, Protector, and Guide, you usually already have another inner voice: the parent you inherited from how you were treated. It can be warm, but for many people its first version is a critic or warden: don’t cry, don’t be needy, don’t get angry, don’t embarrass us, don’t become too independent.
sections.heading: The Parent You Inherited

sections.excerpt: Start With Whatever Showed Up The cynical voice, numbness, urge to scroll, anger, dissociation, or sudden need to do something else all belong inside the pl/ork. The response may be a protector, the child speaking directly, an inherited critic, a present-day grievance, or a blend. Start with what it is trying to prevent, accomplish, or communicate before dec
sections.heading: Start With Whatever Showed Up

sections.excerpt: Two Common Protective Patterns Two patterns often do have a protective function. Proactive protection stays on duty most of the time: the skeptic, intellectualizer, inner critic, or voice watching for weakness and self-indulgence. It may have spent years preventing humiliation, deception, overwhelm, or another abandonment. It has probably watched you begin o
sections.heading: Two Common Protective Patterns

sections.excerpt: A Bottom-Up Sequence Notice the protective part. Don’t push through it. Offer it the same Nurturer voice you intended for the child. “I see you. I know you’re trying to protect something. I want to understand.” Borrow that voice from somebody safe when you can’t generate it yourself. Ask what it expects will happen if it steps back. The answer may be: “This
sections.heading: A Bottom-Up Sequence

sections.excerpt: When the Urge to Escape Arrives Sometimes the protective response is a sudden desire for a substance, a relationship, a new project, or anything else that can move attention away from pain. Don’t shame the urge. Notice what it may be signaling: something painful has come close enough to require management. That can be progress. Thank the protective part. Slo
sections.heading: When the Urge to Escape Arrives

sections.excerpt: Sometimes There Isn’t a Clear Child Yet Reparenting assumes there is a coherent inner child to love. For many people, there is. For others—especially people raised in controlling families, rigid religious environments, or any setting where belonging required performing someone else—the authentic child-self may never have had room to form. The performed self
sections.heading: Sometimes There Isn’t a Clear Child Yet

sections.excerpt: From Survival to Experimental Play When childhood is organized around avoiding pain and preserving attachment, attention goes into reading danger, meeting other people’s expectations, and keeping the bond. There is much less room for the ordinary experiments that answer, “What do I like? What do I want to try? Who am I when nobody is grading me?” Identity gr
sections.heading: From Survival to Experimental Play

sections.excerpt: Untangling the Belonging Bargains Identity formation also requires untangling from family emotional systems, religious orthodoxies, group identities, political tribes, and individual relationships that pull you away from your own knowing in exchange for belonging. Most social systems ask for some conformity. Families want a particular kind of son, daughter,
sections.heading: Untangling the Belonging Bargains

sections.excerpt: Let the Child Be Bad at Things Reflection can reveal what was suppressed, but identity also needs experiments. Try painting, dancing, gardening, a language, a sport, volunteering, music, or something else that has no obvious value to your résumé or social position. Notice what holds your attention when nobody is impressed. The old internal parent may demand
sections.heading: Let the Child Be Bad at Things

sections.excerpt: The Inner Guide Comes Later Key adds the third adult function: the Leader, Guide, or Guru. A competent parent does more than soothe and shield. The parent chooses education and experience, holds standards, requires difficult things for growth, and exposes the child to art, music, beauty, nature, and the wider world. sections.excerpt: A Heart-to-Child Loop If you can feel even a little warmth, put one hand on the center of your chest, at the heart chakra, and feel for love. Put the other on the solar plexus, just below the chest, and feel for the inner child. The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso. One punch there hurts a lot, as I sadly learned while getting beaten up
sections.heading: A Heart-to-Child Loop

sections.excerpt: Journal With Each Hand Write vulnerable thoughts and feelings with your non-dominant hand—the clumsy hand whose script already looks like a child wrote it. Answer with the dominant hand as the adult, offering love, protection, and guidance. This can bypass the silence people hit with speech or visualization. If the protector is what appears, let that part us
sections.heading: Journal With Each Hand

sections.excerpt: Use Childhood Photographs Without Interrogating Them A childhood photograph can help when visualization feels fake. You don’t have to invent the child’s face or posture; you can look at an image from that time. Look gently and notice what arises without deciding what the picture is supposed to prove. Useful questions include: What do I notice in my body? Wha
sections.heading: Use Childhood Photographs Without Interrogating Them

sections.excerpt: When Love Still Feels Missing If you weren’t well-loved as a child, “love your inner child” may sound like nonsense. You may sincerely want the best for the child, hug them in imagination, or miss them—and still feel none of the beautiful warmth people mean by love. Begin with smaller recognitions: Love may already be familiar in another form. Most people ha
sections.heading: When Love Still Feels Missing

sections.excerpt: Hitting the Wall: Radical Acceptance This appears in twelve-step traditions and Zen: stop the self-improvement project for a moment. The effort to fix yourself so you can become worthy keeps reinforcing the belief that you are currently broken. Sit with the loneliness, numbness, or emptiness and say: “This is it. If I never feel love for the rest of my life,
sections.heading: Hitting the Wall: Radical Acceptance

sections.excerpt: Somatic Heart Opening Rumi says you must keep breaking your heart until it stays open. sections.excerpt: The “I Am” Contemplation Advaita Vedanta and non-duality traditions use a different route. Strip away name, job, history, and the identity of “the unloved person.” Attend to the simple fact that you exist. Don’t get stuck at the “I Am” phase; it’s preliminary . The opening comes when existence stops feeling like a neutral fact and begins to feel like infinit
sections.heading: The “I Am” Contemplation

sections.excerpt: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy Learn to do inner-child therapy sober, in your ordinary mindstate. When you’re ready, my self-hypnosis guide or lucid-dreaming guide can take it deeper. Low doses of entheogens can also synergize: cactus, CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, Loveyhuasca , iboga , and others. The gate matters. Altered states can get past the
sections.heading: Altered States Can Deepen the Therapy

sections.excerpt: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow Some people have the opposite problem: they believe they’re connecting when the contact is staying near the surface. sections.heading: When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow

sections.excerpt: How to Forgive Without Forgetting For many people, healing eventually includes some form of forgiveness or release from active resentment. It can’t be required on schedule, and it isn’t a prerequisite for safety, accountability, boundaries, justice, or recovery. Active resentment can narrow what you see and keep the child organized around the injury. Pressur
sections.heading: How to Forgive Without Forgetting

sections.excerpt: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship Reparenting is usually framed as something you do alone or with a therapist. The child was wounded in relationship, though, and a relational injury can only heal so far in isolation. Hearthwork , my peer-counseling framework, begins: Equal time. Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing. You speak. I listen. Then
sections.heading: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship

sections.excerpt: You Are Worthy of Love. Always. Sometimes self-love begins as warmth. Sometimes it begins as borrowed care, a boundary, a meal, a phone put down, or one sentence you are willing to repeat without believing yet. You don’t have to feel like a parent before taking the first adult action. The role can begin outside you, become shared, and then become yours. Smal
